name: Kriang
catalog_citation: Gehrmann, Ryan (2017). The historical phonology of Kriang, a Katuic language. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (JSEALS) 10(1): 114-139. University of Hawai'i Press (CC-BY). hdl:10524/52402.
catalog_locator: p. 117, Section 2 'Phonological description', paragraphs 2-3 (PDF page 4 of the JSEALS bitstream; saved file our source folder/gehrmann2017_historical_phonology_kriang_J…
catalog_quote: The canonical Kriang word may be monosyllabic or disyllabic. In disyllabic words, the second syllable, or the main syllable, is stressed and equivalent in its phonotactics to monosyllables. The unstressed first syllable of a disyllabic word, or the presyllable, is deficient in comparison to the main syllable in that its inventory of permissible initial and final consonants is severely limited and in that it does not carry a phonemic vowel. The Kriang phonological word shape may be summarized as follows: (P1(P2).C1(C2)V(ː)(F) A presyllable must contain a P1 onset but a P2 coda is not required. If no P2 coda is present, an epenthetic central vowel [ɐ] is inserted between P1 and the main syllable onset C1. If a P2 coda is present, then the epenthetic vowel is inserted between P1 and P2.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kriang words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (presyllable + main syllable); stress always falls on the main syllable, which is word-final; the presyllable is unstressed with a predictable epenthetic [ɐ]. Hence word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. The author notes presyllables with other initials occur mainly in expressives, Lao loans (e.g. /mɐlɛŋ/ 'cancer') and reduplications, but says nothing about their stress; words longer than two syllables are not discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (mono- or disyllabic citation forms). Description explicitly 'accounts for both KK and KTT' dialects, with examples mainly from Kriang Tha Taeng; Klor (=Khlor) is a Kriang dialect per ISO CR 2018-008 by the same author but is not separately described.
new_statements.identity_note: khlo1239 'Khlor' [llo] is a retired code: ISO 639-3 CR 2018-008 (Gehrmann) retired it as a duplicate of Kriang [ngt] — Klor [klɔːr] is a Kriang dialect spoken only in Ko' village, Sekong province, 'completely mutually intelligible with Kriang'. Glottolog now has the language-level node ngeq1245 'Kriang-Khlor', which is a separate target in WORLD_TARGETS (scan verdict SOURCE-NAMED-UNREACHABLE naming this same Gehrmann 2017 paper; no files held there). The quoted statement describes Kriang as a whole (both Kriang Kaleum and Kriang Tha Taeng dialects, examples mainly KTT), not Klor specifically. sources.note: p.117, Section 2 (synchronic phonology, valid for both dialects KK and KTT): in disyllabic words the second (main) syllable is stressed; the first syllable (presyllable) is unstressed, phonotactically reduced and carries only a non-phonemic epenthetic [ɐ]. Word template (P1(P2)).C1(C2)V(ː)(F). No mention of secondary stress.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority (2018). Change Request Number 2018-008: retire [llo] Khlor (equivalent to [ngt] Kriang); submitted by Ryan Gehrmann (Payap University), adopted 2019-01-25. SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Establishes identity: 'Khlor is a dialect of Kriang.' Gehrmann met a Klor speaker (Ko' [kɔʔ] village, Sekong province) who 'reported that Klor is completely mutually intellibile with Kriang and that he considers the Klor to be Kriang'; name pronounced [klɔːr], unaspirated.

sources.note: p.13, sec. 2.1: Ngeq disyllables are sesquisyllabic, 'They consist of a pre-syllable (also known as a reduced/minor syllable) which precedes the main syllable. These pre-syllables are typically unstressed, have simple structures and typically include a reduced vowel nucleus (Alves 2006).' No dedicated suprasegmental section; consistent with main-(final-)syllable stress but phrased generically. Data from KK-descended speakers near Pakse (Chalam Chakam dialect).
